newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Brown seen raising taxes in budget.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Brown seen raising taxes in budget.

text.p: British finance minister Gordon Brown is widely expected to raise taxes to slow Britain's surging economy when he unveils the first budget by a Labour government for 18 years on Wednesday.

The centrepiece of the budget will be a windfall tax on the profits of utility companies that Labour believes were privatised too cheaply by the Conservative government that it swept away in the May 1 election.
The money will be used to finance one of Prime Minister Tony Blair's main election promises -- a programme to get 250,000 under-25s off welfare and into work or training.
Brown has also promised to pay for a reduction in tax on home heating bills by scrapping tax relief on private medical insurance for the over-60s.
His speech was also expected to contain measures to encourage long-term investment.

But speculation has intensified in the run-up to the budget that Brown will raise billion of pounds in additional tax with the twin aim of accelerating the decline of the government's deficit and slowing growth in consumer spending and house prices to a less dangerous pace.

The Financial Times reported that Brown would raise more than two billion pounds ($3.3 billion) in tax this year and much more in coming years in order to balance the government's books within five years.

Brown, the workaholic son of a Scottish churchman, gave little away on the eve of the budget, promising only that it would be about "equipping this country for the future" and "meeting the people's priorities".
The Labour government has chalked up record approval ratings in its first two months of office, and the London stock market continued to show its confidence on Wednesaday.
After soaring 2.7 percent on Tuesday, blue chip shares registered another 1.3 percent rise in the first hour of trading before slipping back.
Brokers attributed the jump to hopes that a tight budget will avert the need for sharply higher interest rates to cool Britain's booming consumer sector.

Shares rose strongly despite speculation that Brown will hit pension funds by phasing out a tax credit they get on dividend payments. Scrapping the credit altogether would cut the funds' income by about 3.5 billion pounds, giving Brown a tidy sum to shore up Britain's cash-strapped schools and hospitals.

Home-owners were also braced for bad news. Brown was expected to reduce tax relief on mortgage interest payments -- criticised as a middle class tax break by Labour leftwingers -- and to double tax on purchases of expensive houses.
As a symbol of the government's commitment to environmental protection, Brown was also expected to raise taxes on petrol and company cars.
Members of parliament started queueing as early as 4:00 am to get ringside seats for one of the great traditional spectacles of the parliamentary year.

But Brown has already shown that he is no respecter of tradition -- making the Bank of England independent within days of taking office -- and is poised to make a clean break with some of the customs and rituals of budget day.
Instead of carrying his budget speech in a battered case used since 1860, Brown will use a new red leather budget box made for him by apprentices in his Scottish constituency.
Instead of availing himself of the Cheancellor of the Exchequer's right to fortify himself with a glass of strong liquor during his lengthy speech, Brown intends to sip only Scottish mineral water.
And in a final touch, Brown is likely to walk from his residence at 11 Downing Street instead of being driven the short distance to parliament.

There was also speculation that Brown might soon have another momentous announcement -- the Daily Mail said the chancellor would soon marry Sarah Macaulay, the 33-year-old joint managing director of a public relations firm.
